title: A Movie About What Happens When the Party’s Over
text:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. 

 Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Fiza Kuzhiyil, an assistant editor on the Community team who works on Rabbithole , the magazine’s daily trivia game.

 Fiza has dedicated her year to a timeless read: Anna Karenina . She also enjoys the movie Club Kid , playing Overcooked 2 with her brother, and visiting the Rothko Chapel when she goes home to Houston.

 — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor 

 The Culture Survey 

 The last thing that made me cry: Club Kid —a touching story about what happens when the party is over. This film is the grown-up version of the only Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson movie I have ever seen: the 2007 Disney classic (at least in my household) The Game Plan . Rather than depicting the queer party scene as a hedonistic trap, Club Kid celebrates it as a source of real joy and community. This film feels like the Uber ride home after a party, so how could I—someone who cries at the end of a hangout because I’m so grateful for my friends—not leave in tears?

 The last thing that made me snort with laughter: Also Club Kid . If you’re as online as I am, you’ll roll your eyes at the meme-speak, but it’s impossible not to laugh when you get the references—the kind that make you feel seen, then immediately worried about your screen time.

 Best novel I’ve recently read: Instead of setting a numerical reading goal this year, a friend and I decided to commit to one great, long classic: Anna Karenina . When people ask me if I’ve read anything good recently, I almost always skip over it, not because it didn’t rank, but because what more is there to say than Anna Karenina is the best novel of all time? I can hardly add to what these 19th-century Russian characters have already described about the emotions that I also know—emotions so familiar, they transcend language. Reading it showed me how everyone who came before me has expressed the same thrills, fears, and heartbreaks that I have. The joy of experiencing this novel comes not from deep revelations of plot, but from immersing yourself in the lives of these characters; or, in Leo Tolstoy’s own words, “Pleasure lies not in discovering truth, but in seeking it.”

 A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: “Oh, What a World,” by Kacey Musgraves is always my reminder to be quiet, listen to the world, and take note of my senses. Its counter in my life is the rhapsodic “Trinidad,” by Geese, which is my reminder to accept the tension buzzing among everything I see, hear, and touch. That being said, my loved ones don’t find it amusing when I let go of these tensions by randomly yelling the lyrics to this song (“THERE’S A BOMB IN MY CAR”).

 A musical artist who means a lot to me: Lorde’s four-year music-release cycles have aligned perfectly with major chapters of my life. I made a big cross-country move listening to Pure Heroine , spent late nights in high school with Melodrama , emerged from the pandemic bubble with Solar Power , and started my first years out of college with Virgin . I saw her three times on her most recent tour, and each time, she sang and spoke about the same themes many artists do— love, loss, youth, autonomy —but the rawness and precision in her delivery has always affected me a step above the others.

 A painting, sculpture, or other piece of visual art that I cherish: The Rothko Chapel in Houston, both a nondenominational meditative space and an art exhibition, is the only place of worship I visit regularly. I was lucky to have lived on the same street as the chapel for some time. Whenever I feel disoriented or untethered, a quiet moment with the blackout triptychs feels baptismal.

 Something I recently revisited: My Beatles album ranking—I was always a Sgt. Pepper girl, but I think I’m entering a Rubber Soul time of my life.

 A piece of journalism that recently changed my perspective on a topic: Some of my D.C. friends call me the one-woman Houston Department of Tourism—which is to say that I won’t shut up about Houston or Texas. Inevitably, non-Texans ask me about Buc-ee’s, the behemoth of a gas station. For a while, its outsize Texas-ness felt like a point of cultural pride; I liked being asked about it. But Forrest Wilder’s essay in The Baffler about the company’s water-rights battles and the cost taxpayers incur for its expansion changed the way I felt about letting Buc-ee’s represent me or my state. I may still wear my beaver-printed running shorts, but I think differently about allowing a corporation to serve as a cultural marker.

 My favorite way of wasting time on my phone: I am delighted by the recent obsession with browser games among my friends. Krillion rewards obscure and rare answers with more points, which, frankly, panders well to my uniqueness complex. I also spend too much time playing Catfishing , but I consider it “research” for the trivia questions I write for The Atlantic ’s Rabbithole game (shameless plug).

 Something delightful introduced to me by a kid in my life: Overcooked 2 . I don’t know if I’d call the game itself delightful, because I often take breaks so as to not get too angry, but I am delighted by how my little brother and I are forced to communicate better when we play it. I once preferred the soothing music and satisfying chopping of Cooking Mama on Nintendo DS, but my brother put me on to the new wave of cooking games: cooperative, stressful, and fast-paced. A major perk of our large sibling age gap is that our daily functions rarely overlap, so we have few reasons to get mad at each other. But through Overcooked , we have finally found a way.

 The Least Productive Day of the Year

 By Sophia Nguyen 

 Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off. First, she chalked it up to “personal reasons.” Then she said her birthday was coming up. But eventually, she came clean: She wanted to play Grand Theft Auto VI right when the game dropped, on November 19. Rogers had big plans—decorating with neon lights, stocking up on energy drinks, adorning those drinks with little paper umbrellas. She and her fiancé were going to play until their eyes gave out.

 She didn’t have to worry: Her boss admitted that he was taking time off for the same reason. “I don’t think the company’s even going to be up and running for probably two or three days,” Rogers told me. If you’ve got a metal roof that needs replacing in south-central Texas, it just might have to wait.
